children: Wheat for March delivery fell 1% Tuesday on the Chicago Board of Trade to $5.89 1/4 a bushel, with pre-first notice day selling and a strong U.S. dollar seen weighing.
Soybeans for January delivery rose 0.4% to $12.34 a bushel.
Corn for March delivery edged up 0.1% to $4.50 1/4 a bushel.

Early Signs: The U.S. winter wheat crop was 95% planted as of Sunday with 54% in good or excellent condition, up from 53% the previous week, the Agriculture Department's latest crop progress report showed. "That's now a 10% improvement in good/excellent ratings since their initial estimate, painting a very different picture of this year's crop," Mike Castle of StoneX said in a note. "We've seen a dramatic improvement in soil moisture profiles across the Plains this fall, but it's worth noting that soft wheat areas, both in the eastern Midwest and Pacific Northwest, have been on the dry side lately," he said. Although harvest isn't until the summer, it pays to keep an eye on the status heading into dormancy, Castle added.

Mystery Buyer: The soybean market is still wondering which country President Trump was referring to when he told CNBC on Monday that he had made an "unbelievable trade deal" and that "they're going to buy much more soybeans, much more everything." Some think China, while others have their doubts. AgResource said it doesn't see the deal involving China which has already committed to buying 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans, "and additional supplies would further strain the state reserve system." The firm said it suspects the deal could involve the European Union or Mexico.

Steady Ethanol: U.S. ethanol production was likely steady last week at 1.125 million barrels a day, compared with 1.126 million barrels a day the week before, according to the average estimate of analysts surveyed by Dow Jones. Forecasts range from 1.10 million barrels a day to 1.15 million barrels a day. Ethanol stocks are also seen little changed at 24.9 million barrels, with estimates that range from 24.3 million barrels to 25.2 million barrels.

Export Competition: With the U.S. corn harvest 94% complete as of Sunday, attention shifts to demand prospects and weather conditions in South America, analysts at Rabobank said in a report. U.S. exports have been weak so far, but it's still early in the season. "Reinvigorating U.S. export sales in the absence of meaningful weather risks materializing in South America, against a backdrop of a weaker Brazilian real, would likely require the U.S. FOB premium to narrow from current levels," they said.

Food for Thought: Food inflation in advanced economies has been subdued despite this year's energy shock, in contrast to 2022 when the Russia-Ukraine war led to a 6 percentage-point increase after 10 months, Capital Economics's chief global economist Jennifer McKeown said in a note. Likely reasons include Russia and Ukraine being major global suppliers of agricultural commodities, whereas the Middle East is largely a food-importing region.

Ample inventories of agricultural commodities entering the conflict with Iran helped cushion the effect of higher input costs, while stretched incomes led to intense price competition among supermarkets, keeping them from passing on higher costs. "Food inflation will probably rise as higher energy costs feed through, but it should remain far below its 2022 peaks," McKeown said.
The EIA will release its Weekly Petroleum Status Update report at 10:30 a.m. Wednesday
The USDA and the CBOT will be closed in observance of Thanksgiving on Thursday.
The USDA will release its weekly export sales report at 8:30 a.m. ET on Friday.
The CBOT will be open for a half-day of trading, closing at 1:05 p.m. ET on Friday.
